subsystems.name: Local sensing and perception
subsystems.role: lets each robot know its own position and what is immediately around it.

subsystems.name: Peer-to-peer communication
subsystems.role: exchanges short messages between nearby robots without a central hub.

subsystems.name: Coordination rules
subsystems.role: the local decision rules that produce global swarm behaviour.

subsystems.name: Task allocation
subsystems.role: divides work among robots using only local information.

subsystems.name: Human–swarm interface
subsystems.role: lets an operator set goals, monitor progress and intervene.

buildSteps.title: Define the global goal
buildSteps.detail: Specify what the swarm must achieve, such as covering an area or moving goods, and the constraints like time, energy and safety.

buildSteps.title: Design local rules
buildSteps.detail: Write simple rules for each robot using only local sensing and neighbour messages, often inspired by ant colonies or bird flocks.

buildSteps.title: Simulate at scale
buildSteps.detail: Run thousands of virtual robots to see whether the rules produce the desired collective behaviour and to tune parameters.

buildSteps.title: Implement on robot hardware
buildSteps.detail: Port the rules to embedded controllers on real robots, respecting limited compute, memory and battery.

buildSteps.title: Test with small groups
buildSteps.detail: Run a few robots in a controlled arena to check communication, collision avoidance and basic coordination.

buildSteps.title: Scale up and field trial
buildSteps.detail: Increase the number of robots and move to realistic environments such as warehouses or disaster sites.

buildSteps.title: Deploy with oversight
buildSteps.detail: Operate the swarm with human monitoring, logging and the ability to pause or recall robots.

buildSteps.title: Iterate and harden
buildSteps.detail: Fix failure modes like communication dropouts or stuck robots, and improve robustness over many runs.

prerequisites.why: robots need to talk to neighbours without a central access point.
each robot must be simple and cheap enough to field in large numbers.
emergent behaviour is hard to predict, so testing in software first is essential.
mixing different robot types makes protocol design and testing harder.
simple robots have limited battery life, so coordination must be energy-aware.

pathway.milestone: small swarms with centralised or hybrid control in warehouses and drone light shows
fully decentralised protocols for tens to hundreds of robots in logistics and inspection
pathway.unlocks: scalable fleets that do not rely on a single point of failure.

pathway.milestone: heterogeneous swarms for search and rescue, agriculture and environmental monitoring
pathway.unlocks: teams of air, ground and water robots working together.

pathway.milestone: thousands of micro-robots for precision tasks
pathway.unlocks: collective construction, pollution cleanup or infrastructure repair.
